structure.title: V. Local Development and Structural Transformation
Journal back matter (Nemmers Prize call for nominations; not part of the article)

observations.statement: States three linked designs: an industry-level difference-in-differences comparing manufacturing industries by reparations exposure, a Norway-based triple-difference check, and a municipal shift-share exposure measure used in local and individual-level equations.
observations.locator: Section IV, equation (2); Section V.A, equation (5)

observations.statement: States the identifying assumption for the industry-level design as parallel counterfactual development between more and less exposed manufacturing industries absent the reparations, tested with preperiod balance and trend regressions.

Argues that measuring local exposure from preexposure 1939 industry labor shares, rather than actual reparations factory locations, addresses the concern that the state may have preferentially assigned production to locations it wanted to develop.

Motivates the triple-difference specification using comparable Norwegian data as a check against the concern that reparations-type industries could have grown faster from general postwar European reconstruction demand rather than the Finnish policy itself.

Notes in a footnote that continuous treatment intensity requires a stronger parallel-trends assumption than binary treatment, citing the relevant methodological literature, and reports a binary above-median treatment version in the appendix as a check.

Compiles several newly digitized historical data sets from Statistics Finland's original publications, spanning industry-level, municipality-level, and individual-level data covering roughly four decades around the reparations episode.

States a distinct unit of observation for each empirical layer: the four-digit manufacturing industry for the industrial analysis, the municipality for the local analysis, and the linked individual for the individual-level analysis.

Uses proprietary individual-level administrative census data from Statistics Finland, including a systematically sampled subset of 1950 household census cards and full national census extracts from later decades, linked by encrypted identifiers.

Describes linking individuals across census waves using unique encrypted social security numbers, and separately linking children to their fathers within the same 1950 census household to build an intergenerational sample.

Treats the more established timber and paper reparations industries as a separate category throughout and reports every main estimate both with and without them, arguing they faced a different type of exposure than the underdeveloped heavy industries.

Defines the industry-level treatment as the value of reparations shipped by an industry scaled by that industry's prewar labor force, standardized to a unit standard deviation, to proxy both the size of the shock and the state aid needed relative to existing capacity.

Constructs the municipal-level exposure measure as a shift-share combining 1939 preexposure industry employment shares in the municipality with each industry's reparations shipments, scaled by the industry's initial national labor force.
Measures the main industrial development outcomes, production value, labor force, and value added, on a logarithmic scale in the baseline specifications.
Deflates all monetary production and value-added variables to a constant prewar year of Finnish marks before constructing the industry panel.

Splits industries and local exposure into high-skill and low-skill categories using a published measure of historical U.S. industry average years of schooling mapped onto corresponding historical industry groups, to probe which sectors drive results.
Main regression tables list included fixed effects as indicator rows and report the number of observations and the number of underlying industries or municipalities at the bottom of each table.

Presents columns that progress from a baseline specification to versions omitting established industries, using an alternative treatment scaling, or splitting treatment by skill intensity, within the same table.
States the standard error type and the exact clustering level in the notes beneath every main results table rather than in the body text of the results discussion.
observations.locator: Table III notes; Table VIII notes

observations.statement: States that municipal-level regressions are weighted by an early-period census population figure, both for the local shift-share specifications and for the education-institution regression.
Reports the sample mean of the dependent variable at the bottom of the individual-level and municipal-institution tables, a convention that is absent from the industry-level tables.
observations.locator: Table VIII; Table X; Table XI

observations.statement: Clusters standard errors at the level treatment varies for each analysis: industry for the industry-level design, industry-country for the triple-difference, and municipality for the local and individual-level designs.
observations.locator: Section IV, equation (2); Section V.B.1, equation (8)

observations.statement: Gives no separate paragraph justifying why standard errors are clustered at each chosen level, beyond stating the clustering level alongside each estimating equation, and does not discuss cluster-count adequacy or wild-bootstrap correction.

States that it follows recent methodological literature on shift-share inference and provides the associated robustness checks in an online appendix table set, without reproducing the checks in the main text.

Reports an industry-level balance table with both prereparations levels and prereparations trends of baseline characteristics regressed on the standardized treatment intensity, presented in the main text before the main results table.

Reports an analogous municipality-level balance table with preperiod levels and changes in observable characteristics regressed on the standardized local exposure measure, controlling for region and urban fixed effects.

Presents flexible year-interacted event-study figures for both the industry-level difference-in-differences and the Norway triple-difference side by side with confidence bands, to visually assess pretrends.

Reports cohort-specific event-study estimates for individual-level education and occupation outcomes in an online appendix figure rather than the main text, measured relative to an omitted middle-aged cohort.
observations.locator: Section VI.B.2; Online Appendix Figure A.III

observations.statement: Summarizes robustness of the industry- and local-level baseline estimates to alternative control sets and specifications in a short main-text subsection, with the full tables placed in an online appendix.
Reports an alternative log-with-zeros estimation approach for outcomes with many zero counts, following a recently published methodological paper, as a check on the baseline log-linear specification.
Checks that the upward-mobility results are robust to widening the low-education father sample and to alternative control sets, including nonlinear controls, reported in an online appendix table.
Points to a dedicated set of online appendix tables implementing recently proposed shift-share-specific robustness and inference diagnostics, citing the methodological papers that motivate them.

Splits treatment intensity by industry skill level throughout the industry, local, and individual analyses to test whether high-skill or low-skill reparations exposure drives the results, motivated by an argument about advanced-sector upgrading.

Uses a cohort-age interaction, comparing younger and older individuals at the start of the episode, to test differential effects on education and occupation, motivated by an argument that younger cohorts had more scope to respond to new opportunities.

Splits the intergenerational mobility sample by father's education level and separately reports estimates for children of the least-educated and most-educated fathers to characterize which families benefited most from upward mobility.
Expresses at least one estimated education effect as a share of the outcome's sample mean to communicate its economic size relative to the baseline rate.

Interprets the upward-mobility pattern, in which effects concentrate among children of less-educated fathers, in light of an established growth-and-inequality argument from the historical economics literature.
Explicitly flags that an estimated within-manufacturing productivity effect is imprecisely estimated, rather than presenting it as a null equivalent to zero.

Acknowledges that the within-manufacturing productivity estimates could be biased because sectors might retain or add labor as a consequence of productivity gains rather than the reverse, complicating a causal reading of that specific result.

Notes that the local difference-in-differences and the Norway-based triple-difference local estimates are not perfectly comparable because of differing sample years, countries, and control sets across the two exercises.

States explicitly that the analysis does not claim local industrialization could not have occurred absent the reparations policy, framing the estimated effect as an acceleration of a process rather than a strict counterfactual of no development.

Cautions that the parent-income channel is difficult to interpret causally because both the child's education and the parent's income are themselves outcomes of local reparations exposure, so the mediation exercise is only suggestive.
Uses year- or cohort-interacted coefficient plots with shaded confidence bands as the standard way of presenting dynamic treatment effects across the industry, local, and individual analyses.
observations.locator: Figure III; Figure V; Online Appendix Figure A.III

observations.statement: Includes a choropleth map of the municipal-level exposure measure by quartile to visually convey the geographic distribution of reparations intensity before presenting local-level regressions.

Uses a conventional three-tier significance-star convention and states the corresponding significance thresholds together with the standard error clustering level in the notes of every regression table.
observations.locator: Table III notes; Table XI notes

observations.statement: Labels online appendix tables and figures with an A- or D- prefix distinct from the main-text roman-numeral tables, and states the sample and unit of observation at the start of each main table's notes.

Provides descriptive summary statistics, including means, minima, and maxima of key variables, jointly with balance-test coefficients in the same industry- and municipality-level tables rather than in a separate summary statistics table.

Previews the three-part empirical structure, industry-level, local, and individual-level analysis, along with the general direction of the findings, in the introduction before any results are formally presented.
Closes the introduction with an explicit roadmap paragraph naming each subsequent numbered section and briefly stating its content.
Places a unified data section before any of the three design-and-results sections, so all data sources are described once rather than being reintroduced separately within each empirical section.

Collects robustness checks, additional linkage analysis, heterogeneity, and further extensions into one later numbered section that relies heavily on online appendix tables and figures rather than interleaving them with the main results sections.

Includes explicit contribution paragraphs in the introduction that separately situate the paper relative to the industrial-policy literature, the persistence-of-economic-activity literature, and the intergenerational-mobility literature.
Uses local manufacturing power usage as a proxy for capital accumulation to provide intermediate-outcome evidence for the investment channel underlying the local industrialization result.

Tests a new-institutions channel for the education results by regressing the presence of vocational and higher-education institutions in a municipality on local exposure, using a purpose-built institutional data set.

Frames the parent-income mediation exercise for the education channel as suggestive rather than causal, given the acknowledged endogeneity of both the mediator and the outcome to the same exposure variable.

Follows an established methodology for measuring upstream and downstream industrial linkages to test whether more exposed municipalities also developed a broader base of related industries beyond the initially targeted sectors.

Discusses in a footnote how Finland's much lower industrial base and income level relative to a comparable U.S. wartime-investment study limits direct comparison of magnitudes across settings, while noting a qualitatively similar intergenerational pattern.

Uses the Norwegian comparison to argue that the observed industrialization pattern within Finland was not an inevitable feature of the postwar period, bearing on how far the finding should be generalized beyond the reparations episode.
States a formal data availability statement citing a public Harvard Dataverse replication package with its own DOI, placed immediately before the reference list.

Distinguishes the publicly archived replication package from the underlying proprietary individual-level administrative census microdata, which are described as accessed through Statistics Finland rather than redistributed in the public package.
Credits a named collaborator for jointly digitizing the municipal manufacturing survey data in a footnote, documenting the provenance of one of the historical data sets.

concordance.paper_says: Baseline industry-level regression is described as a difference-in-differences OLS model with industry and year fixed effects (equation 2), estimated on a four-digit industry panel.
concordance.card_shows: s1-s3 are traced as reghdfe (Stata hdfe OLS) with absorb(year isic ...), matching equation (2).

concordance.paper_says: States industry fixed effects and year fixed effects, plus 1943 controls interacted with year effects, in the baseline industry-level specification.
concordance.card_shows: s1.fixed_effects records ['year','isic']; the interacted elastic-net controls named in the paper are not captured as a separate structured field (only an unresolved macro appears in the raw command).

concordance.paper_says: States that standard errors are clustered at the industry level in the industry-level difference-in-differences.
concordance.card_shows: s1.se.cluster_level records ['isic'], matching vce(cluster isic) in the traced Stata command.

concordance.paper_says: States country-industry and country-year fixed effects for the Norway triple-difference (equation 4).
concordance.card_shows: s4.fixed_effects records ['year_country','isic_country'], matching absorb(year_country isic_country) in the traced command.

concordance.paper_says: States that the triple-difference standard errors are clustered at the industry-country level.
concordance.card_shows: s4.se.cluster_level records ['isic_country'], matching vce(cluster isic_country) in the traced command.

concordance.paper_says: States municipality and year fixed effects plus region and urban fixed effects interacted with year for the local shift-share difference-in-differences (equation 8).
concordance.card_shows: s7.fixed_effects records ['year#laani50','year#city','year#town','code'], an interacted region/urban-by-year and municipality-code structure consistent with, though not identical in exact form to, the paper's stated fixed-effect list.

concordance.paper_says: States that the local-level regressions in equation (8) are weighted by 1939 municipal census population.
concordance.card_shows: s7.weights records an aw=wei weight variable, consistent with population weighting, though the card does not resolve which population year the weight variable uses.

concordance.paper_says: States that local-level standard errors are clustered at the municipality level.
concordance.card_shows: s7.se.cluster_level records ['code'], the municipality code variable, matching vce(cluster code) in the traced command.

concordance.paper_says: States that the upward-mobility regressions (equation 15) cluster standard errors at the 1939 municipality level.
concordance.card_shows: s8, s9 and s10 each record se.cluster_level as ['muni_g'], a municipality grouping variable, matching cl(muni_g) in the traced command.

concordance.paper_says: Describes several explicit comparison groups in prose: nonexposed manufacturing industries, Norwegian industries and municipalities, and industries or municipalities split by skill intensity.
concordance.card_shows: comparison_group is recorded as null on every traced design and specification.

concordance.paper_says: Describes elastic-net-selected 1943 or 1940 control variables interacted with year or cohort fixed effects in detail, naming specific variables such as skilled-worker share and average wages.
concordance.card_shows: controls_summary is null on every traced specification; the raw command text shows only an unresolved control-list macro ($sharecontrols) rather than a structured control list.

concordance.paper_says: Reports industry- and municipality-level balance and pretrend tables (Table II, Table V) and multiple event-study figures as design diagnostics in the main text.
concordance.card_shows: the card's diagnostics array is empty.

concordance.paper_says: Describes a substantial robustness program (Section VII.A) covering alternative controls, specifications, binary treatment, log-with-zeros, and shift-share-specific checks, mostly detailed in an online appendix.
concordance.card_shows: the card's robustness array is empty.

concordance.paper_says: Associates each specification with a named table or figure throughout the results sections, for example Table III, Table VI, and Table XI.
concordance.card_shows: the card's top-level outputs lists are empty, though individual specification 'notes' fields informally record some table and column references, for example s1's note cites Table 3, Column 1.

gaps: No preregistration, IRB approval, or participant-consent statement of any kind appears in the read text (category preregistration_or_ethics is entirely absent).

No explicit statement of analysis software or version (for example Stata and its version) appears in the main text; software names such as reghdfe are only visible in the replication code, not in the prose.
No R-squared is reported in any of the main regression tables read (Table III, IV, VI-XI); tables report N and, for some, the dependent-variable mean instead.

No explicit discussion of cluster-count adequacy, wild-bootstrap correction, or other few-cluster inference concerns appears in the main text despite the industry-level and triple-difference specifications having a moderate number of clusters.
No explicit multiple-hypothesis-testing correction is discussed in the main text across the many outcome families examined (education, occupation, income, institutions).

The paper's Online Appendix (identification checks, most robustness tables, heterogeneity detail, and shift-share-specific diagnostics referenced throughout) is a separate document not included in this text extraction and was not read; its existence and general content are recorded only as stated by the main text.

reading.note: All 65 pages of the provided text were read in full, including the introduction, historical background, data, all three empirical sections (industry, local, individual), the further-analysis/robustness section, conclusions, the data availability statement, and the reference list (pages 60-64, read to confirm bibliography-only content and locate the data availability statement). Page 65 is unrelated journal back matter (a Nemmers Prize call for nominations), not part of the article. Coverage is recorded as main_text rather than full because the paper's Online Appendix, cited extensively for diagnostics, robustness, heterogeneity, and shift-share-specific checks, is a separate document not included in this text extraction and so could not be read; its content is recorded only as described by the main text.
